name: Lilac
lede: Lilac is the pale, slightly pinkish purple of the lilac blossom, a word with a dark blue ancestor that was the common-speech name for the first mass-market purple dye.

sections.title: The flower and the word
sections.body:
The color is named for the common lilac, a shrub whose flower clusters run from near-white through pale purple to a pinkish mauve [1]. Paterson defines the word as the pale purple of lilac blossom, and traces it through *anil*, the old name for indigo-yielding plants, to the Sanskrit *nila*, dark blue [1]. So a pale purple word has a dark blue ancestor.

As an English color word, lilac is recorded from 1775 in the sources behind our library [15]. It then climbed steadily in print: Google Books counts for the adjective rose fastest in the 1840s and peaked in the 1890s [14]. The timing matters, because those are the decades in which a synthetic purple dye made pale purples fashionable.

Our swatch is a light, slightly pink purple, `#C8A2C8` [15]. ISCC-NBS files lilac in its block 222, "light purple", about five ΔE units from this swatch [15]. Our nearest named neighbors are [[pink-lavender]], [[hay-s-lilac]] and [[wisteria]] [15].

sections.title: A dye before it was a craze
sections.body:
Lilac was the plain-English word Greenfield uses for the first result of Perkin's coal-tar experiment [6]. Greenfield reports that on silk the black residue gave a shimmering lilac, which Perkin called Tyrian purple and which became known as Perkin's mauve [6]. The chemistry is told in the [[mauve]] article; what matters here is that lilac was the everyday word for how the result looked.

The word appears in the dye trade before the craze had a name. A dye-trade correspondent wrote to Perkin that that the best lilac then available on cotton came from one house in the United Kingdom, Andrews of Manchester, who could charge any price because even theirs was not quite fast [5]. The letter says Perkin's dye stood up to tests that theirs did not [5].

When the fashion arrived, the two words traveled together. The *Illustrated London News* described a royal dress as mauve, adding "lilac" in brackets, as though readers needed the older word to understand the new one [3]. A later report on the craze called mauve an exquisite shade of lilac [3]. Garfield reports that the British Colour Council later suggested seven fashionable shades based on Perkin's first color, including one called "purple lilac" [4]. Garfield also notes that mauve itself runs from lilac to lush purple depending on the speaker, which is why the two names are so often swapped [18].

sections.title: Which lilac
sections.body:
Lilac has never been one fixed color, and the references show it. Ridgway's 1912 plate gives a lilac a little bluer and lighter than ours, `#CEACDA` [15], while the xkcd color survey (2010) settled on a much bluer, more saturated `#CEA2FD` [15]. The same name covers a pinkish wash and a bluish lavender.

Other dictionaries stretch it further. St Clair's glossary lists *periwinkle* as a lilac-blue, *mallow* as a pinky lilac, and *pearl* as a very pale lilac-gray [10]. Paterson also records the adjectives *lilaceous* and *lilacky* [1]. Each of these uses lilac as the anchor and shifts it a little toward blue, pink or grey.

The pale-purple family is crowded. Compared with [[lavender]], lilac in the ISCC-NBS system is a lighter, pinker purple [15], and [[wisteria]] and [[thistle]] sit close by on screen [15]. The helpful habit for the eye is to ask which way the purple leans, toward pink or toward blue, and to name it with the matching neighbor: [[blue-lilac]] for the cooler side, [[pale-lilac]] for the paler and greyer.

sections.title: A basic color word in waiting
sections.body:
Berlin and Kay's scheme of basic color terms includes purple and pink [9]. A 2015 online naming experiment by Dimitris Mylonas and Lindsay MacDonald argued for adding two more: turquoise and lilac [9]. That is a proposal from one study, not an accepted change, and Westland reports it as a claim that makes a case rather than as settled fact [9].

The interest of the result is practical. The study's claim, in effect, is that English speakers keep a separate category for a pale, cool purple, one that does not collapse into [[pink]] or into [[purple]] [9]. The word that fills it is a flower name [1].

sections.title: Lilac in nature's charts
sections.body:
Syme's revision of Werner's color chart, which Baty reproduces, uses the word twice [7]. Syme's "Bluish Lilac Purple" (number 35) is described as bluish purple and white, and is matched to a dragonfly, the lilac shrub's blue form and the mineral lepidolite [7]. His "Red Lilac Purple" (number 43) is matched to light spots on a peacock butterfly's wings, a pale purple primrose and lepidolite again [7].

The pairings show what the word meant to a naturalist of that period [7]: a pale purple, tinted by white, that the eye would find in a flower, an insect and a mineral alike.

sections.title: Lilac in painting
sections.body:
Painters rarely mix lilac from a single violet pigment. Ball points out that Rembrandt's portrait of Hendrickje Stoffels (about 1654 to 1656) can look like a pale lilac dress [8]. Yet there is no blue in it [8]. The violet tint comes from lead white and charcoal black, which together read slightly blue, warmed by a little red lake [8]. The lilac is a product of the surrounding colors, not a pigment.

A French critic quoted by Gage, writing about a painter's work, mentions some lilac on a cushion and a lilac of exquisite freshness in a fabric, using the word for a bright decorative accent [12]. Gage also quotes Bracquemond on the fashionable color names of his day, including one that could mean anything from pink to lilac or even yellow, and which has left no trace [12]. Color names of this kind show how loose the lilac region of language is.

sections.title: Lilac before lilac
sections.body:
Long before the word, there are hints of pale purple materials. The Pigment Compendium records that Spurrell in 1895 reported "lilac" compounds from an Egyptian blue workshop at Tell el-Amarna, and that contemporary experiments suggested such a pigment could be made by varying the firing temperature [11]. The compendium notes the chemistry is unclear and that barium copper silicates have not been reported from Egypt [11].

A better-documented purple is Han purple, a barium copper silicate found on Chinese artifacts of the Han dynasty and the Warring States period [11]. The compendium calls it almost unique as a pre-industrial, inorganic, true purple pigment [11].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, a lilac like this swatch covers at least one per cent of the canvas in only four paintings, and in only two when the match is held to the stricter within-painting lens [13]. That makes it rarer than 82 per cent of our named colors [13]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the numbers describe the archive, not painting as a whole.

Among the dated matches, the earliest is a work by [[painter:paul-serusier|Sérusier]] from 1894, and the latest is from 1914 [13]. That fits a color word that only became common in print in the later nineteenth century [14]. With four paintings the pattern is thin, and a match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test [13].
